props.title: Faces
props.initialSlug: Marriage crumbles in raw portrait of 60s suburbia

sections.content: **Faces** (1968) represents John Cassavetes' masterful dive into middle-class American desperation. Shot in stark 16mm with intense close-ups, the film follows a married couple's disintegration through a night of separate encounters. Cassavetes pioneered a raw improvisational style that influenced generations of independent filmmakers, from Martin Scorsese's **Mean Streets** (1973) to the Safdie brothers' **Uncut Gems** (2019). The handheld camera work and naturalistic performances created a template for intimate character studies that still feels revolutionary today.

sections.content: The film's influence on American independent cinema cannot be overstated. Its DNA runs through **Husbands** (1970), Cassavetes' follow-up exploration of masculine crisis, through to contemporary works like **Marriage Story** (2019) and **Malcolm & Marie** (2021). The unvarnished examination of human relationships, shot in intimate close-ups with natural lighting and overlapping dialogue, created a new cinematic language for depicting emotional truth.

Gena Rowlands and John Marley's performances set new standards for naturalistic acting. Their work influenced the development of method acting and can be traced through films like **Blue Valentine** (2010) and **Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?** (1966). The film's exploration of suburban ennui and marital discord laid groundwork for later works like **Revolutionary Road** (2008) and **In the Bedroom** (2001). sections.content: Cassavetes' use of handheld cameras and natural lighting influenced both narrative and documentary filmmaking. The film's technical approach can be seen in works like **Medium Cool** (1969) and later in Danish Dogme 95 films like **The Celebration** (1998). The raw immediacy of **Faces** created a bridge between documentary and narrative storytelling that continues to influence filmmakers like Sean Baker (**The Florida Project**, 2017) and Kelly Reichardt (**Certain Women**, 2016).
